subject: biology
title: Factors affecting transpiration and the potometer
key_idea: Transpiration is faster when it is warmer, brighter, windier or less humid. A potometer measures the rate of transpiration by how far an air bubble moves as a shoot takes up water.

sections.heading: What affects the rate of transpiration

blocks.text: Four environmental factors change how fast water is lost from the leaves: light intensity, temperature, air movement and humidity.

rows: Photosynthesis happens and the stomata are open.
Moving air blows the water vapour away from the leaf.
A greater water vapour gradient between the leaf and the air.

diagram.alt: Pick a change in conditions to see what happens to the rate of transpiration.

options.label: Brighter light
results: Stomata are open and photosynthesis happens.

options.label: Darkness
results: No photosynthesis, so the stomata are closed. Very little water is lost.

options.label: Cooler
results: Evaporation is slower, and the stomata are almost closed.

options.label: Windier
results: Moving air blows water vapour away from the leaf.

options.label: More humid
results: A smaller water vapour gradient between the leaf and the air.

items: Stomata are almost closed at night, so less water is lost.
The upper surface of a leaf is warmer, drier, more exposed to wind and has more light, so it has fewer stomata.
Answers should be comparative: say faster or slower, more or less.
More light, higher temperature, more wind and lower humidity all increase the rate of transpiration.
In the dark the stomata close, so there is very little transpiration.
Always give a comparative answer and a reason.

sections.heading: Measuring water uptake with a potometer

blocks.text: A potometer measures how much water a shoot takes up. Water uptake is used to measure the rate of transpiration.

items.text: Fit a cut shoot into the potometer. Fill the apparatus with water and put an air bubble in the capillary tube.
Position the bubble at 0 mm. Record the position of the bubble every minute.
Repeat in different conditions, such as moist air or dry air, or with a fan on or off.
The further the bubble moves in a given time, the faster the water uptake.

items: Capillary tubing is narrow, so the bubble moves further and a small change in volume is easier to see.
Control the other variables: temperature, light intensity and wind.
A heat sink between the lamp and the plant absorbs heat, so the temperature stays constant.
Repeat readings and find a mean. An anomalous reading does not fit the pattern.

blocks.label: Volume of water taken up
where: r = radius of the capillary tube in mm (half the diameter)
l = distance the bubble moves in mm

blocks.label: Rate of water uptake
blocks.formula: rate = volume of water taken up ÷ time

diagram.alt: Practise calculating the volume of water taken up from the distance the bubble moved.
diagram.question: A potometer has a capillary tube of diameter **{D} mm**. The air bubble moves **{L} mm**. Calculate the volume of water taken up by the plant. Use π = 3.14.

items: A potometer measures water uptake from how far the bubble moves.
Change one factor at a time and control the others.
Volume = π × r² × l, with the radius half the diameter.

checks.q: Give two factors that affect the rate of water loss from leaves, other than temperature.
checks.a: Any two from: humidity, air movement (wind), light intensity.

checks.q: The air bubble in a potometer would not move in the dark. Explain why.
checks.a: There is no photosynthesis, so the stomata are closed. So there is no (or very little) transpiration.

checks.q: Explain why narrow tubing is used in a potometer.
checks.a: The air bubble moves further in a given time, so a small change in volume is easier to see.

worked_example.question: A student used a potometer to investigate the rate of water uptake in a plant shoot. As the shoot takes in water the air bubble moves. The investigations were carried out in daylight. The air bubble would not move if the investigations were done in the dark. Explain why.
answer_points: There is no photosynthesis, because plants need light for photosynthesis.
So the stomata are closed, because no carbon dioxide is needed.
So there is no transpiration (or very little water is lost).
worked_example.tip: Link the three steps in order: no light, stomata closed, no transpiration.

worked_example.question: A scientist investigated how the flow of air affected the rate of transpiration in a plant. A fan was used to change the flow of air. The volume of water taken up by the plant was measured. Give one reason why the volume of water taken up by the plant was also measured when the fan was not switched on.
answer_points: To compare the effect (of the fan with no fan).
As a control, or to get a baseline measurement.
worked_example.tip: Either answer scores the mark. Say the reading with no fan is what the other readings are compared with.

worked_example.question: A simple potometer is used to investigate the effect of light intensity on transpiration rates. The mean distance the gas bubble moved along the tube at 10 cm from the light was 72 mm. The diameter of the narrow tube was 1 mm. Calculate the volume of water taken up by the plant. Use the equation: volume = πr²l, where r is the radius of the tube and l is the distance the bubble moves. π = 3.14. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
worked_example.tip: Using 1.0 as the radius gives 226.08, or 230 when rounded. These score only 1 and 2 marks. Rounding correctly to 2 significant figures earns a mark.
